title: Brussels Unveils Chips Act 2.0 as Iranian-Linked Hackers Hit 30 US Water Systems
subhead: The EU rolls out its biggest tech sovereignty package yet, while a suspected Iran-linked cyber campaign against Minnesota water utilities exposes the soft underbelly of US critical infrastructure.

sections.heading: EU Launches Tech Sovereignty Package: Chips Act 2.0, a Cloud-and-AI Act and an Open Source Strategy
sections.body:
The European Commission formally presented its European Technological Sovereignty Package, bundling two legislative proposals — Chips Act 2.0 and the Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) — with an Open Source Strategy and a Strategic Roadmap for Digitalisation and AI in Energy, according to the Commission's digital-strategy portal.

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen framed the push bluntly: 'We cannot afford to depend on others for the technologies that keep our hospitals running, our energy grids stable and our services secure.' The Commission says the package is designed to cut structural dependencies as AI drives a sharp rise in compute demand.

Chips Act 2.0 aims to accelerate permitting (approvals within a maximum of 12 months), introduce 'Grand Challenges' for strategically important chips such as AI accelerators, and add 'Demand Accelerators' to link manufacturers with industrial buyers. The Commission credits the first Chips Act with mobilising more than €52 billion in public and private investment and creating an estimated 46,000 jobs, while conceding the EU remains dependent on third countries for advanced manufacturing and design. It projects the global semiconductor market to reach €1.37 trillion by 2030, with AI-related components driving roughly 70% of that growth.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe is trying to convert demand-side leverage into domestic capacity — but the package arrives as earlier deadlines slipped and EU AI experts are already urging the bloc to triple its AI compute share. Legislation is the easy part; the fabs and cloud capacity are not.

sections.heading: Suspected Iran-Linked Cyber Campaign Hits 30+ Minnesota Water Systems
sections.body:
Federal investigators are probing a suspected cyberattack on more than 30 community water systems across Minnesota, after malicious activity disrupted operations and forced several utilities to switch to manual controls, according to WION and Cybernews. State officials say four cities have publicly confirmed the attacks.

Investigators are examining whether the hackers have links to Iranian cyber groups. The FBI has cautioned that findings remain preliminary, and officials are also weighing whether the attackers deliberately tried to appear Iran-based amid heightened US-Iran tensions. The attribution has become politically contested: President Trump publicly blamed Minnesota itself rather than Iran, while Governor Tim Walz's office pushed back, per Gizmodo and IBTimes UK.

The incident follows a pattern of prior cyber probes against US utilities tied to alleged Iran-linked groups, and it lands days after British police arrested suspects over an alleged plot against RAF Fairford, a US bomber base in the UK, with possible Iranian involvement under investigation (Metro, Times of India).
sections.whyItMatters: Water systems remain the weakest link in US critical infrastructure — numerous, under-resourced, and running legacy OT gear. The disputed attribution shows how quickly a technical investigation becomes a political fight, which slows coordinated defense.

sections.heading: China Weighs Letting ByteDance and Alibaba Buy Nvidia's RTX PRO 5500
sections.body:
China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has asked major domestic firms including ByteDance and Alibaba to submit procurement plans for Nvidia's RTX PRO 5500 chip, signalling Beijing may authorise the purchases, according to The Information (relayed by ChinaTechNews, Reuters and Yahoo Finance).

Industry executives expect the RTX PRO 5500 to sidestep US export limits. ByteDance is reportedly targeting roughly one million units, driven by domestic demand that exceeds what Huawei and other local suppliers can provide; Nvidia reportedly plans 500,000 units in quarterly shipments beginning this December. An Nvidia spokesperson said US firms 'continue to be restricted by a combination of outdated US export controls, which cover gaming products released nearly a half a decade ago, and China's own limits on US imports.'

The move cuts against the grain of Beijing's self-reliance drive and follows reports that Huawei's Ascend chips have pushed Nvidia's China market share down sharply. Analysts read it as a rationed stopgap rather than a full reopening.
sections.whyItMatters: Beijing is quietly conceding that domestic silicon still cannot meet its AI demand — a pragmatic exception to its own autonomy push. For Nvidia it is a partial re-entry; for Huawei it signals that the political cover for import substitution has limits when compute is scarce.

sections.heading: China's CPPCC Convenes to Chart Total Tech Self-Reliance Under the 15th Five-Year Plan
sections.body:
China's top political advisory body, the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), convened non-party intellectuals and officials in Beijing on Sept. 21 to plan an accelerated push toward technological self-reliance, according to ChinaTechNews.

Wang Dongfeng, CPPCC vice chairman and secretary-general, urged delegates to align research with national priorities under China's upcoming 15th Five-Year Plan, calling for deeper structural reforms in science and technology and faster breakthroughs in digital and intelligent technologies. Economist Lin Yifu and other standing committee members attended; the Ministries of Education and Science and Technology briefed attendees on progress and bottlenecks.

Notably, the meeting leaned on non-party academics and private-sector experts to attack hardware and software chokepoints — a sign Beijing sees autonomy as requiring expertise beyond traditional party cadres.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the political scaffolding behind Beijing's semiconductor and AI import-substitution push. It also reveals the gap it is trying to close: even as it rations Nvidia imports, China is formalising a whole-of-society mobilisation to replace them.

sections.heading: China Accelerates a Commercial Space Surge — Hainan Hits 23 Sorties, Megaconstellations Advance
sections.body:
China's commercial aerospace sector is pivoting from policy-driven research to a high-cadence industrial engine, with the domestic commercial space market projected to surpass 3.5 trillion yuan ($495 billion) in 2026, per ChinaTechNews.

The Hainan Commercial Space Launch Site has completed 23 successful launch sorties and recently supported the orbital flight of the Long March 10B, which achieved what officials describe as the world's first sea-based net recovery of a booster stage. The surrounding Wenchang aerospace complex now pairs rocket manufacturing, satellite assembly and ground-station telemetry, including an automated satellite 'super-factory.'

A new class of 'Type II' defence-industrial entrants — companies with pre-existing missile and rocket designs and state backing — is displacing the venture-funded startups of a decade ago. Kuaizhou Aerospace completed its 40th sortie with the Kuaizhou-11 on Sept. 17 after a 3.3 billion yuan state-led restructuring.
sections.whyItMatters: China is industrialising launch cadence and LEO constellation deployment at scale — the same playbook SpaceX pioneered. High-density sorties plus direct-to-cell and remote-sensing constellations translate into sovereign ISR and communications capacity that is hard to sanction.

sections.heading: Rare Earths Stay Central: US Stockpile Push Meets China's Export Leverage
sections.body:
Critical minerals remain the sharpest instrument in the US-China trade standoff. Reuters reported that the US is investing heavily in critical minerals while China maintains its grip, and that China's rare earths dominance is set to overshadow the Trump-Xi talks. Beijing's Notice 61 (Oct. 9, 2025) required a Chinese export licence for any product made outside China containing Chinese-origin rare earth elements at or above 0.1% of value — among the most aggressive extraterritorial controls ever applied to a raw material, per ChinaTechNews.

On the US side, Trump announced a $12 billion rare earth minerals stockpile, and a Greenland deal plus accelerating stockpile purchases drove sharp moves in junior miners (CRML, GRML). Germany, meanwhile, is reported to be hoarding rare earths as Brussels squares up to Beijing.

The de-escalation measures tied to the Xi-Trump summit are set to lapse in November, keeping the standoff live.
sections.whyItMatters: Rare earths are where China's leverage is most direct and least substitutable in the near term. Stockpiling buys time but not independence — processing capacity outside China remains the real bottleneck, and the November expiry is the next pressure point.

sections.heading: Türkiye Tech Angle: Taurus Satellite Constellation Ready, Space Ambitions Firm Up
sections.body:
Türkiye's homegrown Taurus satellite constellation is reported ready for launch, per Anadolu Agency. The programme sits within a broader national space push: Türkiye has initiated preparations for the TÜRKSAT 7A satellite project and is targeting 2027 for its first lunar mission, according to Anadolu and earlier Turkish space reporting.

On the commercial side, US investment in Türkiye is shifting toward technology and AI, and Istanbul recently hosted the GITEX AI tech event, with AI adoption in the country reported above 50%, per Anadolu and Daily Sabah.
sections.whyItMatters: For Türkiye, sovereign satellite capacity is about both communications independence and the ability to source ISR imagery without foreign gatekeepers. It is a modest but concrete step out of dependence on allied space providers.

bottomLine: Today's thread is sovereignty-by-legislation versus sovereignty-by-capability. Brussels passed its most ambitious tech package yet — Chips Act 2.0 and a Cloud-and-AI Act — but the EU still lacks the fabs and compute to match the ambition, and its own experts want a tripling of AI compute share. China, in the same 24 hours, showed both sides of its position: a CPPCC push for total self-reliance under the 15th Five-Year Plan, paired with a pragmatic willingness to let ByteDance and Alibaba import Nvidia's RTX PRO 5500 because domestic supply can't keep up. Meanwhile the suspected Iran-linked hack of 30+ Minnesota water systems — with attribution already muddied by politics — is a reminder that the most exposed infrastructure is often the least glamorous. Going forward: watch the November expiry of the rare-earth de-escalation and whether China's Nvidia exception becomes policy or stays a rumour.
sources: European Commission digital-strategy portal, The Information (via ChinaTechNews/Reuters/Yahoo Finance), Cybernews, WION, Gizmodo, IBTimes UK, Metro, Times of India, ChinaTechNews, Reuters, Anadolu Agency, Daily Sabah
